summary: This informational document defines Opportunistic Security: protocols use encryption even when authentication is not available, and use authentication when possible. The goal is to remove barriers to widespread encryption, giving some protection most of the time instead of none.

plainLanguage.summary: Opportunistic Security aims to encrypt communication whenever both peers can, even when they cannot verify each other's identity. It uses authentication when that is available and preserves any explicit policy that requires stronger protection.

questions: why not require authentication for encryption
subtitle: Use encryption when peers support it, and authenticate them when reliable identity information is available.

tldr.problem: Protocols that require full authentication and encryption may fail with peers that cannot provide them, leading operators to disable protection and use cleartext.
tldr.mechanism: Opportunistic Security treats cleartext as the baseline, then negotiates encryption and authentication where available, while explicit security policies take precedence.
tldr.outcome: The approach can protect against passive monitoring even when peer identities cannot be authenticated. RFC 7435 is an Informational design document, not a protocol specification.

today: RFC 7435 is an Informational document published in December 2014. It describes a security design approach rather than specifying a protocol.

sections.title: Why Full Protection Can Reduce Protection
sections.content:
Earlier security designs often offered either authenticated and encrypted communication or a hard failure. When users had trouble connecting, operators sometimes disabled the security and used cleartext. The RFC argues that this all-or-nothing choice leaves much communication unencrypted.

Authentication can be difficult when peers do not share a trusted identity system. The memo describes limits of certificate-based trust, trust on first use, and DANE at the time it was written. It argues that encryption without authentication is still useful because it makes passive monitoring harder.
sections.plainLanguage: If a connection works only when both sides can prove their identities, some connections may fail and protection may be turned off. Encryption without identity checks can still stop someone from simply reading the traffic.

sections.title: The Three Possible Security Outcomes
sections.content:
Opportunistic Security uses cleartext as the baseline and negotiates encryption and authentication when available. It does not treat partial protection as a fallback from a promised higher level of protection; it aims to use the strongest protection available for each peer.

A connection may be authenticated and encrypted, encrypted without authenticating the peers, or cleartext. Encryption helps against passive monitoring. Without authentication, a man-in-the-middle attack can still be possible.
sections.plainLanguage: A connection may be authenticated and encrypted, encrypted without identity checks, or unencrypted. The protocol tries for the strongest option the peers can support.

sections.title: Rules for Designing Opportunistic Security
sections.content:
Explicit security policy always takes priority. Opportunistic Security is not meant for data or applications that require authenticated, encrypted communication. It should also be possible to deploy one peer at a time, without preventing communication with peers that support fewer security features.

Use encryption when both peers support it, authenticate when a reliable authenticated source provides the needed keys or credentials, and use perfect forward secrecy where possible. A system must not describe unauthenticated encryption as if it provided authenticated encryption. Capability advertisements need to reflect what the peer can actually do.
sections.plainLanguage: Never override a rule that requires authenticated encryption. For other connections, use encryption when both peers support it and explain clearly whether the peer's identity was checked.

sections.title: Example: TLS for Email Delivery
sections.content:
The RFC uses SMTP mail transfer as an example. An SMTP client can request TLS with the STARTTLS extension after the server advertises support. Because that initial negotiation is not protected, an attacker on the path may remove the advertisement and cause the client to send cleartext.

The RFC says that abandoning encryption because a certificate check fails and immediately reconnecting in cleartext is not consistent with its principles when encryption is still possible. It also describes Opportunistic DANE TLS, which requires authenticated encryption for peers with suitable DANE records and uses Opportunistic TLS for other peers.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail servers can negotiate TLS before transferring a message. If the initial negotiation is not protected, an attacker may hide the offer, so this example does not guarantee encryption against active attacks.

sections.title: Fallback and Remaining Risks
sections.content:
The memo says fallback to cleartext should be enabled only to address significant operational problems. A failed security negotiation may reflect an interoperability problem rather than an attack, but frequent failures can lead administrators to disable Opportunistic Security altogether.

This approach does not stop active attacks when authentication is absent, and some protocols may be vulnerable to downgrade attacks. The RFC says large-scale passive monitoring becomes harder and widespread active attacks are more likely to be noticed. Techniques for detecting and mitigating active attacks without authentication are outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Opportunistic encryption does not prove who is at the other end, and an attacker may interfere with negotiation. Designers should limit cleartext fallback and should not use this approach when policy requires authenticated encryption.

viz.caption: THE THREE OUTCOMES DESCRIBED BY THE RFC

items.title: Authenticated and encrypted
items.text: The peer identity is checked and the communication is encrypted.

items.title: Encrypted, not authenticated
items.text: Passive reading is harder, but a man-in-the-middle attack may remain possible.

items.title: Cleartext
items.text: Communication is unencrypted when encryption is unavailable or not negotiated.
